view: Inwardly, the night signifies the natural self.
Night covers the day with darkness, removing its light.
note: Several notes cite 13:3 or 7:54 for the day as the object.

view: Night covers the sun.
note: Several notes connect this possibility with 91:4.

view: Night covers the earth.
note: Abū Ḥayyān includes all that is on earth.

view: Night covers the world.
Night covers all creatures, encompassing and filling them.
note: The Study Quran says all creation.

view: Night covers everything concealed by its darkness.
note: Some notes cite 113:3. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the verb as intransitive.

view: Night covers the horizon with darkness, extending over everything between heaven and earth.
The covering can fall on grief, or on eyes, hearts, and faculties through sleep and heedlessness.
note: These are additional possibilities alongside physical objects.

view: The phrase can mean that night darkens.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ specifies a covering of deep darkness.

view: Ghishāʾ or yaghshā means covering or veiling.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ traces the root gh-sh-y.

view: The root gh-sh-y also denotes veiling or dulling perception in sleep or fainting, including sight or insight.
note: The cited Quranic usages include rejection, sleep, fainting, and veils over heart and senses.

view: The root gh-sh-y can describe the overwhelming manifestation at the lote tree.
note: The note cites 53:16.

view: The root gh-sh-y often describes Judgment and its punishments covering people, faces, or places.
The root gh-sh-y can name terrors or darkness.
A poem by al-Nābigha compares night to a pursuer who catches the speaker despite the apparent distance of escape.
The object of yaghshā is left unexpressed because the listener can infer it from context.
Leaving the object of yaghshā unspecified lets the covering include every possible object.
note: Naḥḥās calls this deliberate vagueness; Elmalılı says it heightens terror.

view: Yaghshā functions intransitively here, so no object needs to be supplied.
note: The effect conveyed is night covering everything in darkness.

view: Night's darkness conceals what daylight revealed, like a garment, while day clears and exposes it.
note: Quṭb adds that night and day oppose each other in cycle, appearance, qualities, and effects.

view: Night shelters living creatures, stills them, and brings restorative sleep; day sends people, birds, and other creatures out for livelihood.
note: Rāzī says their alternation serves both work and rest, citing 25:62 and 14:33.

view: Night and day are two great signs God alternates over creation.
Night evokes confusion and obscurity, gradually hiding what daylight made visible, and is suited to secrecy.
People seeking secrecy choose night, while those seeking publicity choose day, whether righteous or wicked.
Spiritual light from night prayer and other good deeds will become sensory light after death.
Night signifies cosmic and inward darkness.
Encompassing night can carry a person from differentiation into unity, multiplicity into solitude, and witnessing into annihilation.

Night is the accidental darkness of passing away after existence, rather than primordial nonexistence; the verses evoke the perishing of all except God's face and passage from annihilation to abiding witness.
note: The note cites 55:26–27 and 28:88.

view: The image can warn of a town or people engulfed by punishment, the era of ignorance around the Prophet's mission, death agonies, or resurrection events.
The definite article in al-layl can denote night as a whole kind or one particular terrifying night, literally or figuratively.
The conditional idhā asserts realization; with the imperfect verb, the event may be present or future.
Yaghshā uses the present tense because night covers gradually, while the past tense for daylight's appearing fits its sudden arrival at sunrise.
note: The note compares the verbs in al-Shams.

view: Using a past verb for a present event can make it vivid and immediate, transporting the listener to the event or bringing the event before the listener.
note: The notes illustrate this with 2:144 and 3:21 and say Arabic past forms have several temporal uses.

view: Contrast clarifies meaning: night covers while day becomes manifest.
This verse opens an oath.
The sworn object is the whole night, whichever object of its covering is supplied.
Oaths by natural phenomena establish a premise.
The oaths display the worth of created things and the greatness of their Creator, and direct attention to the coming subject.
Quranic oaths probably draw on a characteristic expression of pre-Islamic soothsayers, though this connection has not been sufficiently studied.
The structure and function of this oath type are linked to 93:1–2 and its parallels.
The night and day oath parallels other early Meccan oaths, especially the wording of 91:3–4; the brightening day corresponds to ḍuḥā in 91:1 and 93:1.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr specifically connects the time restrictions on night and day with the preceding surah's oaths.

view: Oaths by night and day, then male and female, set cosmic opposites alongside diverse human efforts and their contrasting outcomes.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ includes the denier's fire and the pious giver's satisfaction; Neuwirth calls the pairs a structural matrix; Ibn Kathīr connects the male and female with other created pairs.

view: The night and day pair and the male and female pair form two cosmic oppositions; the second oath enigmatically points to God, who speaks explicitly in verses 7–10.
Night and day, like male and female, are complementary pairs: each fills the other's void and together they fulfill their created purpose.
note: The note says the capacity and use of either member make little sense without its counterpart.

view: The harmony of complementary opposites argues for monotheism and, here, for the Hereafter; this world's counterpart completes its purpose.
note: The note cites 51:49.

view: The outer and inner signs in verses 1–4 establish that Judgment must come: the Hereafter is this world's counterpart and gives it meaning.
Night and day's alternation directly affects the soul, evoking the mysterious universe, change, human inability to control it, and a power directing it.
The precise order of night and day shows that a director governs the heavens and human lives and did not create people without purpose.
Even when deniers divert attention, the heart stays connected to the universe and recognizes its director instinctively and through reflection.
Night's darkness alludes to the solar system's original state before daylight followed the sun's creation; reckoning time began with nights before days.
The sūra pairs closely with al-Shams in central themes and inner and outer features.
After the preceding sūra's believer and disbeliever and their outcomes, this sūra presents the contrast again.
This sūra explains which traits produce the success and failure named in the preceding sūra, then warns of the Fire and distinguishes those who enter it from those spared.
note: Iṣlāḥī stresses identifying corruption and protection or purification of the soul.

view: After al-Shams depicts purified and corrupted souls and Thamud's fate, this sūra treats people's divergent good and evil efforts under God's governance through piety and wickedness.
note: Biqaʿī calls God's governance complete and freely chosen despite people's shared aims.

view: The opening oaths summarize al-Shams: that sūra moves from light to darkness, knowledge of God and self, and Thamud's ruin; this one moves from annihilation toward witnessed light, purification, growth, and abiding in God.

The previous sūra ends with warning; this one starts with warning and proceeds to glad tidings. A people's destruction does not diminish the Creator, who can renew creation through day, male, and female.
The omitted object recalls the night covering the sun in the preceding sūra.
note: The note cites 91:4.

view: The name al-Layl signals darkness and sleep, which frustrate ordinary desire; sleep is death's sibling.
Sajā, suggesting both stillness and darkness, suits the pause of revelation and loss of light; yaghshā and yasri suggest movement and fit that setting less well.
note: The note compares 92:1 with 89:4.

view: The case of idhā under coordinated oaths is problematic: making the wāws govern both accusative and genitive, or repeating oath wāws, creates disputed constructions.
note: This is al-Zamakhsharī's reported analysis.

view: Coordinating wāws do not themselves govern case; the first conjunct's governing element governs the later conjuncts too.
note: Abū Ḥayyān rejects the contrary analysis.

view: The construction coordinates genitive and accusative pairs rather than coordinating under two separate governors, as in 'I passed Zayd yesterday and ʿAmr today.'
note: Sībawayh's poetic parallel coordinates a genitive and nominative in the same case pattern.

view: Al-Khalīl treats the first wāw like an oath preposition, but the last two wāws as ordinary noun coordinators.
Al-Khalīl's statement makes the disputed construction prohibited, whereas al-Zamakhsharī describes it as merely disliked.
note: Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Zamakhsharī's characterization.

view: Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir pronounce the relevant verse endings openly in this sūra, al-Layl, and al-Ḍuḥā.
Al-Kisāʾī uses imālah throughout the relevant endings here and in al-Layl and al-Ḍuḥā.
Nāfiʿ's transmitted pronunciations differ: intermediate endings, fully open endings through Warsh and Qālūn, or an open talāhā with the rest inclined.
Abū ʿAmr is reported with intermediate imālah; ʿAbbās transmits full inclination for selected endings, and other transmissions vary across the verse endings.
The Prophet, ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Abū al-Dardāʾ, and Ibn ʿAbbās are reported reading 'the male and the female' without mā.
note: A report in both Ṣaḥīḥs says Abū al-Dardāʾ heard the Prophet read it so and ʿAlqama reported Ibn Masʿūd's same wording.

view: Ibn Jinnī takes the reported reading without mā as evidence for an analysis making the male and female pair genitive in apposition to mā.
Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the prophetic reading without mā as an early permitted variant later replaced by the final reading agreed upon by the reciters and written in Abū Bakr's muṣḥaf.
note: He says al-Zamakhsharī called it the Prophet's reading.

view: Al-Layl was revealed in Mecca.
note: Māwardī says this is unanimous; the other notes also report Medinan or mixed claims.

view: Al-Layl was revealed in Medina.
note: Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī attribute this to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa.

view: Part of al-Layl was revealed in Medina and part in Mecca.
Al-Layl is unanimously counted as twenty-one verses.
Al-Layl is early Meccan and is often placed ninth in revelation order.
The sūra is named al-Layl after its opening oath.
A stingy palm owner denied fallen fruit to poor children; a believer exchanged forty palms for that tree and gave it to the family after the Prophet promised its owner a palm in Paradise.
note: Ibn Kathīr's account says the original owner refused the Prophet's offer.

view: The palm transaction and charitable buyer occasioned the revelation of this sūra's opening and its contrast between giving and withholding.
Ibn Kathīr calls Ibn Abī Ḥātim's palm story very unusual.
Most reports connect the sūra's revelation with Abū Bakr; sound chains are cited from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and others.
Ibn Masʿūd reports that Abū Bakr bought Bilāl from Umayya ibn Khalaf for a cloak and ten uqiyyas, freed him, and the opening of this sūra was revealed.
note: Ālūsī gives the broader Abū Bakr attribution; the Bilāl transaction details are from Ibn Masʿūd.

view: Al-Suddī links revelation to Abū al-Daḥdāḥ's charitable purchase of a palm for orphans.
note: Ālūsī says al-Suyūṭī judged the associated Ibn ʿAbbās report weak.

view: God first created light and darkness, then distinguished them as dark night and bright, seeing day.
A prophetic report promises reciters of al-Layl contentment, protection from hardship, and an easy path.
The Prophet rebuked Muʿādh for a long prayer and instructed him to recite shorter sūras, including ones beginning with glorification, the sun, dawn, and night.
The Prophet instructed recitation of both al-Layl and al-Shams in the dawn prayer.
God may swear by any creature, while people may swear only by God.
note: Both are transmitted through Imams called al-Bāqir; the second comes through ʿAlī ibn Mahziyār.

view: Tajallī means appearing or becoming uncovered, with physical senses such as a receding hairline, sight clearing by polish, displaying a bride, or polishing a blade or mirror.
note: Jishumī also gives illumination and clarity.
